claims.text: Pulumi's component state migrations feature lets component authors ship the upgrade path with the component itself.
A Pulumi component state migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.
Pulumi component authors can change the internal design of a component and include the state migration in the same release.
The Pulumi component state migrations API is experimental and may change.
A GitHub discussion for component state migrations feedback exists at github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ covering component state migrations and the callback contract.
The pulumi/examples repository contains a directory aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration with the AWSX VPC state migration example containing all three programs (v1, v2, v3) and the migration code.
A Pulumi docs page exists at /docs/iac/concepts/components/ describing components.
The legacy AWSX VPC component manages the VPC, subnets, route tables, and gateways.
The legacy AWSX VPC component is `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc`.
In the example's first version (v1), the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway.
Because the security group refers to the VPC's ID, replacing the VPC would mean replacing the AWS security group too (AWS CloudFormation docs for EC2 SecurityGroup VpcId).
Without a migration connecting old state to new code, an upgrade from legacy to modern AWSX VPC could replace the VPC instead of keeping it.
The example does not create a database.
If a database is recreated, its replacement does not automatically contain the old data.
The modern AWSX VPC component is `awsx.ec2.Vpc`, and the second version of the example upgrades to it while keeping the existing network.
The third version of the example removes AWSX and declares the resources directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
Across all three versions of the example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same and the security group continues to use the same VPC.

In the example, the Pulumi resource tree for v1 is awsx:x:ec2:Vpc containing aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc, awsx:x:ec2:Subnet (with subnet, routeTable, routeTableAssociation), and awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway (with internetGateway); v2 is awsx:ec2:Vpc with the aws Vpc, Subnet 'vpc-isolated-1', RouteTable, RouteTableAssociation and InternetGateway beneath the Vpc; v3 has aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc at the root with the same children.
In Pulumi state, each record has a Pulumi name called a URN, and managed resources also have an ID from the cloud provider.
Legacy AWSX wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components, while modern AWSX removes those wrappers and puts the managed resources under different parents.
In the example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1` between legacy and modern AWSX.
Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible.

The legacy-to-modern AWSX upgrade needs to remove component wrappers and transfer references to replacement resources, which aliases alone do not handle, whereas a state migration describes that whole change together.
Pulumi component registration accepts a `stateMigrations` option that takes a migration callback, and an alias for the legacy component type.
The example's `migrateClassicVpc` function is in the file aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts in pulumi/examples.
With a state migration, the alias lets Pulumi find the old component, and the callback receives the component's saved state followed by the state of its children.

A Pulumi state migration callback returns two things: `newState`, the complete set of records that replace the old component and its children, and `successors`, a map from each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place.

The example's migration callback is safe to run again: if the state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources it does nothing, and an unexpected component type raises an error instead of guessing.
The example's `rename` helper copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent, preserving the AWS resource ID and other saved fields.
The Pulumi engine uses the `successors` mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack, including a security group's reference to the VPC outside the VPC component.
The two subnet entries in `successors` tell the Pulumi engine that the old component wrapper and the managed subnet point to the same new subnet record.
The VPC successor mapping keeps the security group's reference connected to the migrated VPC record, which retains the same AWS VPC ID.
The third version of the example declares the VPC, subnet, route table, association, and internet gateway directly with `@pulumi/aws`.

The second migration in the example (v3/migration.ts) removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place, mapping both the old component and its VPC child to the new VPC record, with the VPC keeping its AWS ID.
The second migration is located at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v3/migration.ts in pulumi/examples.
The example's VPC registration keeps aliases for both previous component types and both migration callbacks.
Pulumi runs state migration callbacks in order, passing each result to the next callback.
A stack still using legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to the plain AWS version, and a stack already using modern AWSX skips the first migration.
Once both migrations have run, both callbacks return no result on later updates.
Keeping earlier migrations with the component means its users can skip versions without editing stack state by hand.
A state migration changes saved state; afterward Pulumi compares the new program with that state and calls the provider for any remaining changes.
In the example, the upgrades can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags even though resource IDs are kept.
To try the example, start with `v1` and follow its README, using the same stack, backend, project name, AWS region, and availability zone for each version.
Running `pulumi preview` before each example upgrade should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group.
`pulumi preview` evaluates the state migration without saving it, and the update (`pulumi up`) saves the migrated state.

When a component registers its migration inside its implementation, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit their stack state; Pulumi runs the migration as part of the normal preview and update.
For an internal component change that keeps the same inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls without knowing which resources moved.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the stateMigrations resource option) run during previews and updates when prior state exists.
Pulumi state migration callbacks must be idempotent and return no result when the state no longer needs migration.
Pulumi state migration callbacks rewrite state without performing provider operations.
A Pulumi component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A Pulumi component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
In a component state migration result, each successor mapping connects an old URN omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a component state migration callback returns no result.
The stateMigrations resource option reference documents the callback API at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/#callback-api.
The state entries passed to a component state migration callback use the Pulumi checkpoint resource format, including fields such as urn, type, id, parent, provider, inputs, and outputs.
A component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using update plans or targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing results of component state migrations (under update plans or targeted updates) do not require removing an already-applied migration.
